Why would a king pay a man to do nothing but watch a clock? In 1490, Prague did exactly that. And the reason was money, not time.

The clock on the town hall was a promise. It told merchants that the city could count, plan and pay its debts. When the hands slipped, traders from Nuremberg laughed at Prague.

But one winter morning the clock stopped. Nobody knew why. The keeper took the gears apart one by one and found a crack as thin as a hair. A new wheel took three weeks to cast.

For three weeks the square lived without time. Market stalls opened late. The cathedral bells rang early, then late. The council finally saw what one crack really cost.

So it hired a second keeper. Now two men checked each other every day. Mistakes became rare, and the clock became the pride of the city.

Five hundred years later, the gears have been replaced, repaired and saved from a fire in 1945. Yet one rule never changed: someone always answers for the clock.

What is the one thing in your life that works only because somebody looks after it every single day?
